ideas.title: Boundary-only help budget with affinity-gated mutation cycles
ideas.sketch: After generation, fit Plackett-Luce to a first sparse round of rubric-frozen pairwise judgments and bootstrap each idea's rank interval. The fixed 'T-helper' budget of critique and development calls goes only to ideas whose 80% rank interval straddles the top-3 cutoff: at most H=6 per cycle, with none for clear winners or clear losers. Each helped idea gets one justified critique naming its weakest rubric criterion. A mutator then writes k=3 variants, each a single targeted edit to that weakness and never a fresh idea. Each variant replaces its parent only if it beats the parent and the current rank-3 idea in blinded pairwise judgments against the frozen brief-plus-rubric; losers are discarded. The loop runs R=3 cycles or stops early when the cutoff set stops changing. The on/off test compares this with uniform development of the same top-6 at an equal token budget, scored by benchmark win rate against the single agent's top 3. A per-cycle parent-versus-child win rate gives a measured in-run signal. Why one agent can't match this: a lone agent refines ideas it already favours, while this loop spends effort only where independent relative judgments say the top-3 decision is still open. Honest transfer rating: strong for budget targeting and survivor mutation. Weaker for 'fixed antigen', because an LLM judge is a noisier and more biased affinity measure than binding energy, so it needs length-capped cards and counterbalanced order.

ideas.title: Memory compartment of successful mutation operators, not ideas
ideas.sketch: Each parent-versus-child contest in a mutation cycle is a measured outcome: did the edit raise affinity on the frozen rubric? In the idea library, store these records as memory B cells: tag each edit with an operator type from a fixed taxonomy (e.g. narrow scope, swap mechanism, add a falsifiable test, merge with a rival's strongest component, invert an assumption, cut cost), plus the brief's embedding and the criterion it targeted. This is plasma versus memory: the run's top 3 go to the user, while operator win statistics carry forward. In later runs the mutator picks operators by Thompson sampling over Beta posteriors from the library's win and loss counts, weighted by brief-embedding similarity (cosine above 0.6), instead of free-form 'improve this' edits. Test: for a held-out sequence of briefs, compare operator memory on against a uniform-operator control at equal cost. Outcomes are benchmark win rate and the within-run child-beats-parent rate, which is a direct measure independent of the final raters. Transfer caveat: immune memory stores binders tied to specific antigens. Storing transferable edit types instead is a deliberate departure, because ideas rarely carry over between briefs but good refinement moves may. The effect shows only over many runs, so gains on a single brief will be small at first.

ideas.title: Portfolio selection of the top 3 by posterior expected-maximum with mechanism-cluster correlation
ideas.sketch: Replace 'take the 3 highest Bradley-Terry / Plackett-Luce scores' in the final selection step with a set-selection rule. Draw K=2000 posterior samples of the score vector (bootstrap over the pairwise comparisons, refit BT each time). Have one cheap role-agent label each finalist with a mechanism cluster (which core lever the idea pulls, not its topic). Add a shared cluster-level random shift to the sampled scores so that ideas in one cluster are positively correlated, as they will be in practice. Then greedily pick the 3-set that maximises the mean over samples of the best idea in the set, with a tie-break towards more distinct clusters. This corrects a real failure of top-3-by-score: near-duplicate winners that succeed or fail together, which wastes the slots. A single agent that self-selects 3 from its own 20 tends to pick 3 variants of its favourite theme and has no posterior to hedge with. Test it on/off in the scoring module only, with everything upstream identical. Measures: best-of-3 and mean rated score against the blinded panel, and the number of distinct clusters in the delivered top 3. The gain concentrates on briefs where raters disagree or where outcomes are heavy-tailed, and the change adds no judge tokens beyond one labelling call.

ideas.title: Loss-conditioned revision with a monotone acceptance test and a fixed card budget
ideas.sketch: Add a revision loop after the first pairwise round. Each finalist's developer receives the judges' written reasons from the comparisons it lost, and must fix only the specific weakness those reasons cite. Hard constraint: the revised card has the same token budget as the original, so a revision cannot win by growing longer or more polished. The revision is then tested against its own original in a position-swapped pair judged by a different model family from the generator and the developer. It is accepted only if it wins both orderings, otherwise the original stays. Accepted revisions re-enter the Plackett-Luce fit as replacement items. This is hill-climbing with a verifier. It gives the pipeline something a single agent lacks, which is an independent adversary's stated reasons for why an idea lost, and it protects against the usual failure of self-revision, where 'improvements' are cosmetic or dilute the idea. Test it on/off at the development phase: the fraction of revisions accepted, and the blinded panel's ratings of final cards revised versus unrevised. A word-count-matched control and a family-swapped rater panel check that the gain is not from length or style.

ideas.title: Claim ledger: objections must ship an executable check, and survival is the passed-check count
ideas.sketch: Add a 'claim_extraction' step at the start of the critique phase in which a neutral extractor agent rewrites each idea sketch into a numbered ledger of falsifiable claims (quantities, feasibility bounds, 'no one has done this', dependency assumptions), typically 4-8 per idea. Each critic must then attach to every objection exactly one of three check artifacts: (a) a sandbox Python script (30 s CPU, no network) that prints PASS/FAIL against a stated tolerance, e.g. a Monte Carlo or dimensional/back-of-envelope calculation of the claimed quantity; (b) a library lookup that returns the nearest past ideas above a cosine-similarity threshold of 0.85 together with their recorded pairwise win-rates and prior falsifications; or (c) a declared 'not checkable', which the state machine records but assigns zero weight. The state machine executes the checks, and the idea's survival score into development is s = (#claims passed) - 2*(#claims falsified), with critic prose withheld from the selector so argument eloquence cannot move the score. The benchmark measure is outcome-based: run the same extractor-plus-checker over both the system's top 3 and the single agent's top 3 and compare the falsified-claim rate; the change is switched off by reverting to prose-only critique with identical token budgets. One strong agent cannot match this because it does not have a library of past outcomes and does not run its own falsifiers against its own claims; the gain sits in critique and selection.

ideas.title: Check-repair development loop with a cross-run library of reusable check templates
ideas.sketch: Restructure the development phase into a bounded repair loop: the developer agent receives only the ledger entries that FAILED or were INCONCLUSIVE in critique (not the critic prose) and must either revise the idea so the same check passes on re-execution or delete the claim from the card; at most 3 iterations, after which any still-failing claim is struck. Every executed check is stored in the idea library as a template triple (claim pattern, sandbox code, outcome) keyed by claim type, and before writing a fresh check the developer or critic must first query the library for templates whose claim pattern matches at cosine > 0.8, reusing and parameterising them so that check quality accumulates across runs rather than being re-improvised. Final cards therefore contain only claims that have passed a run check, and no 'verified' badge or check text is shown to raters, so the improvement must show up in idea substance rather than in polish. Measurement is on/off (repair loop vs one-shot development with equal tokens) with two outcomes: the falsified-claim rate of the top 3 under a held-out checker using a different model family, and the number of claims struck per idea as a diagnostic of how much the loop is doing. This targets development directly and improves each run by borrowing checks from previous ones, which a single self-selecting agent cannot do.

ideas.title: Calibrated selection head trained on the library's blinded benchmark verdicts
ideas.sketch: Extend the idea library so each past finalist (not only the top 3) stores a fixed feature vector x: per-criterion critic scores, internal Bradley-Terry strength from the pairwise finals, development-stage score change, generator/role id, embedding distance to the nearest library idea, and nuisance covariates (card word count, number of hedges/citations, judge-model-family match). For each benchmarked brief, label finalists with the blinded external outcome: win/loss against the baseline agent's self-selected top-3 cards (humans or measured outcomes weighted 3x over the LLM panel). To get about 10 labels per brief rather than 3, run the counterbalanced panel on all finalists once. Fit an L2-regularised logistic model P(beats baseline | x) = sigmoid(w.x) with leave-one-brief-out cross-validation, and replace the final top-3 cut with ranking by predicted external win probability. Because length and polish enter as explicit covariates, the model can learn to discount judge-pleasing features instead of rewarding them. The ablation is a switch, select_by = internal_BT | calibrated. It is measured by held-out log-loss/AUC of each selector against external verdicts and by the benchmark top-3 win rate on unseen briefs. A lone agent cannot do this: it never learns how its own picks fared, so it has no labelled record of its selection error to correct.

ideas.title: Judge-reliability Bradley-Terry: per-judge discrimination and position bias learned from held-out external outcomes
ideas.sketch: In the scoring module, replace the uniform pairwise-finals Bradley-Terry with a judge-aware model, P(i beats k | judge j, i shown first) = sigmoid(a_j(theta_i - theta_k) + b_j), where j indexes judge model x prompt variant, a_j is that judge's discrimination and b_j its position bias. Estimate a_j and b_j on past library runs, anchoring theta to the external blinded verdicts, i.e. the rater/outcome rankings of the same ideas, by maximum likelihood with an N(1, 0.5) prior on a_j and N(0, 0.5) on b_j. Freeze them for new runs. Judges with a_j near zero or negative (those tracking style or their own model family rather than what raters prefer) are down-weighted automatically. The state machine then allocates the fixed finals comparison budget in proportion to a_j^2 (Fisher information per vote), and among pairs picks those whose theta difference is small near the top-3 boundary. The ablation is a switch between the uniform-weight judge panel and learned weights, at equal comparison count. It is measured by held-out pairwise agreement with external raters, the rank correlation of theta with outcome, and the benchmark top-3 win rate. The gain targets selection: a single agent is effectively one judge of unknown reliability picking its own top 3, whereas this system learns empirically which of its judges predict independent preference.
